message.content: You are joining a reverse-engineering project. First read /tmp/notes/ARCH.md completely — it explains the task, the strict rules (black-box only: never decompile/trace/read the original binary; no internet), the repo layout, and the comparison tools in /tmp/agent-tools/. Your job: implement `lini highlight` exactly. The function to implement is `pub fn highlight(src: &str) -> String` in `src/highlight.rs` (currently a stub that just escapes). `main.rs` already calls it for `executable highlight FILE` / `highlight -` (stdin) and prints the result with `print!` (no extra newline). `--css` is already done. Errors for missing files are already handled. What we know about the original's highlighter (verify everything yourself): - It never fails, even on lexically invalid input (e.g. `@` or an unterminated string are passed through / partially spanned). It preserves the source text exactly (all whitespace/newlines), wrapping recognised tokens in `…` with HTML escaping (& < > " → & < > ") applied to all text, spanned or not. - KINDs seen: comment, string, number, const, keyword, type, type-user, prop, prop-user, var, op, class, punct (see `executable highlight --css`). - It is a quirky state machine, not the real lexer. Examples from `executable highlight assets/test_doc_examples/skill_01.lini` and `skill_07.lini`: in the stylesheet `w = 120;` the name and `=` are NOT spanned; `scale(n) = (100 * 1.2^n)` → `scale`, `n`, `=`, `*`, `^` unspanned but `(`/`)` punct and numbers spanned; `repeat(2)` → `repeat` is `type`; `|svc::box|` → `svc` type-user, `::` op, `box` type; `|box#in|` → `#` punct and `in` type; `.hot` → class; `--teal-wash` → var; `#ff6600` → const; layout keywords like `grid` → keyword; property names → prop; link operators `->` → op; in `plate:left (-) plate:right { side: bottom; }` only the first `plate` `:` `left` and the `(`, `)` are spanned — the rest of that line (second endpoint, braces, `side:`) is NOT spanned the same way; `.2` in `plate.pin.2` is a number. Unknown/user property names probably get prop-user, user type names type-user. Approach: run `executable highlight` on all files under /workspace/assets (test_doc_examples/*.lini, test_doc_examples/blocks/*.lini, test_samples/*.lini) and on many small synthetic snippets you write (in /tmp//), infer the exact state machine, implement it, and iterate until every asset file and your snippet corpus matches byte-for-byte (`cmpw.py /tmp/bin-hl/executable -a highlight `). Pay attention to: comments (`//…` to end of line), strings with escapes, numbers (negative, decimals, `.5`), percentages, hex colours vs `#id`, `--vars`, classes, bars/types/ids, link operators of all shapes (`->`, `-->`, `<->`, `~>`, `-o<`, `+-o<`, `>-`, `*-`, `(-)`, `(o)`, `||`, `-`, `&`), keywords vs prop names vs plain identifiers in different contexts (stylesheet, node style blocks, link style blocks, expressions in parens, function calls like move()/right()/grid()/gradient()), tags like `right(7.2):north`, unicode text, CRLF, tabs, and lexically invalid input. Only edit `src/highlight.rs` (you may add a helper module if really needed). Build with `cargo build --release` in your worktree and copy to `/tmp/bin-hl/executable` to compare. When done, commit on your branch and report the pass rate on the asset corpus and your snippet corpus, plus any known remaining mismatches.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

# Lini reimplementation — notes for contributors

## The task (read carefully)
We are reimplementing, from scratch in Rust (std only, no crates), a closed binary at
`/workspace/executable` ("lini 1.1.0", a diagram compiler: Lini source → SVG). Our build must
produce byte-identical stdout/stderr/exit codes for every input. Hidden tests compare outputs
exactly, so a test only passes when the whole output matches.

RULES (strict):
- Learn behaviour ONLY by running `/workspace/executable` with inputs and reading its output.
  NEVER decompile/disassemble it, never use strace/ltrace/gdb on it, never read its bytes.
- No internet, no looking for lini source code anywhere. std-only Rust.
- Do not run `./compile.sh` in /workspace (it would try to overwrite the original binary).
- Keep scratch scripts OUTSIDE the repo (e.g. /tmp/<you>/). Non-Rust code in the repo is limited.

## Docs / samples
- `/workspace/README.md` (overview), `/workspace/assets/` — sample inputs:
  `test_doc_examples/*.lini` (one per documented property, plus SPEC/SKILL snippets),
  `test_samples/*.lini` (larger feature boards), `test_images/mark.png`.
  The hidden test-suite is very likely more files of the same kinds.

## Build & compare
- In your checkout: `cargo build --release` → `target/release/lini`.
- Copy it to a private dir under the name `executable` (help/usage text uses argv[0]):
  `mkdir -p /tmp/bin-<you> && cp target/release/lini /tmp/bin-<you>/executable`
- Tools in `/tmp/agent-tools/` (shared, read-only use):
  - `cmpw.py /tmp/bin-<you>/executable [-a "args"] files...` → OK n / m and failing files.
  - `dw /tmp/bin-<you>/executable file.lini [args]` → diff (original vs ours).
  - `rr 'lini source' [args]` → run the ORIGINAL on a snippet (prints output + [exit N]).
  - `rm2 /tmp/bin-<you>/executable 'lini source' [args]` → diff on a snippet.
- Font metric helper (python, for exploration): `/tmp/scripts/tw.py` / `/tmp/scripts/ttf.py`.

## Code map (src/)
- `main.rs` — CLI dispatch (`cli.rs` emulates clap), `compile_src()` pipeline:
  parse → `scene::build_sheet` → `scene::Builder` (node tree) → `compile::compute` (cascade +
  `Computed` per node) → `layout::measure(ctx, 0, None)` → `render::render`.
- `lexer.rs`, `parser.rs`, `ast.rs` — tokens / recursive descent / syntax tree. Errors are
  fail-fast: first `Diag` aborts (`diag.rs` has codes & text/JSON rendering).
- `scene.rs` — `SheetModel` (root config decls, vars, bindings, type rules, defines, classes,
  id rules, link rules), `Node` (prim, `chain` = type chain most-derived first, id, classes,
  inline decls, text, children, `props` = cascaded decls map, layout fields w/h = rect size,
  x/y = centre relative to parent centre), `Builder` (statements → nodes).
- `types.rs` — built-in type registry (name, primitive, base, defaults as lini decl text).
- `style.rs` — value helpers (`value_num(s)`, `ident_of`, colour/weight/dash serialisation).
- `compile.rs` — `Ctx` (all state), `cascade()` (type chain base-first: defaults then user
  `|type|` rules; then classes; id rules; inline), `compute()` fills `ctx.comp[i]: Computed`
  (font size/weight/family, padding, gap, direction, align, justify, width/height, stroke…).
- `layout.rs` — `measure()` dispatch (text, line/poly/path geometry, chart hook, grid, flow).
  `outer(ctx,i)` = rect size + stroke width when stroke != none (text: its box).
- `render.rs` — SVG + stylesheet. CSS rules are collected as (slot, text) and sorted by
  `SLOT_ORDER`; families push extra rules into `out.extra_rules`. Root `--lini-*` vars are
  emitted for every var referenced (`use_var(&mut out.vars, name)`), sorted by name.
  The scope class is `lini-scope-` + hash8(style text written with `.lini` as scope).
- `util.rs` — `f4()` (all coordinates: `{:.4}` then trim zeros; "-0"→"0"), `hash8()` (FNV-1a 64,
  folded hi^lo, 8 hex), `xml_escape`, `base64`, `levenshtein`.
- `font.rs` — bundled TTFs (extracted via `--embed-font`); `text_width(family, weight, size, s)`.
- `markers.rs` — arrow/dot/diamond line-end markers. `geom.rs` — SVG path bbox.

## Facts learned so far (all verified against the original)
- Text box: width = Σ advances·size/1000 (+ letter-spacing·(n−1)); height = size for one line,
  n·1.2·size + (n−1)·line-spacing for n lines. Text renders `<text class="lini-text" x y
  dy="0.358em">`; multi-line uses tspans (first y = centre − (n−1)·pitch/2 + 0.358·size).
- Inline `style="…"` on a node = its own/inline decls minus those equal to what its CSS rules
  (type chain + classes) already give, in CSS_ORDER.
- Indentation: 2 spaces per nesting level; scene children start at 4.
- Only the first error is reported (`file:line:col: error: msg`, exit 1); warnings are printed
  before the SVG and do not change exit code (unless --strict).

## Working rules
- Put your feature in its own module(s); keep edits to shared files (main.rs, layout.rs,
  render.rs, compile.rs, scene.rs, types.rs) minimal and additive — other people are editing
  them in parallel and we merge branches afterwards.
- Commit your work on your branch in your worktree (`git add -A && git commit -m ...`) when
  done, and report: what passes, what doesn't, and any shared-file changes you made.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. - `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

#!/bin/bash
# usage: rr 'lini source' [extra args] -> runs the ORIGINAL on the snippet (file r_in.lini in a private tmp dir)
src="$1"; shift
d=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rr.XXXXXX); printf '%s' "$src" > $d/r_in.lini

#!/bin/bash
# usage: rm2 BIN 'lini source' [extra args] -> diff original vs BIN on a snippet
mine="$1"; src="$2"; shift 2
d=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rm2.XXXXXX); printf '%s' "$src" > $d/r_in.lini
cd $d; /workspace/executable "$@" r_in.lini > o1 2>&1; e1=$?; "$mine" "$@" r_in.lini > o2 2>&1; e2=$?

From mindmap to blueprint.

One small language for every kind of figure — pretty by default, precise when it has to be.

lini.rs — the tour, the reference, the gallery, and the compiler in your browser

Thirty-odd lines of Lini — samples/hero.lini.

--- ## What it is A compiler: plain text in, clean themeable SVG out. You say where things go, and the parts you'd rather not do by hand — routing a wire through the gaps, measuring a dimension, picking a palette — are done for you. - **One grammar, every family.** Flowcharts, mindmaps, org charts, tables, ER schemas, sequences, charts, engineering drawings, floor plans, and circuit schematics are all layouts over the same nodes and links. Not ten tools with ten syntaxes — one language, so theming, baking, and diffing work identically in each. - **Themeable after export.** Every colour is a live CSS variable and a `light-dark()` pair, so one SVG follows the viewer's OS with no script and no re-render, and one line of host CSS recolours every diagram on a page. - **Fast and deterministic.** A typical figure compiles in about 2 ms, byte-identical every run, so SVGs diff cleanly in CI. - **No runtime.** A single native binary. No Node, no headless browser, nothing to stand up beside it. - **Agents can write it.** [`SKILL.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/SKILL.md) is the whole language as a working brief, and the property schema is generated from the compiler's own ledger. ## Gallery
Charts
 ER schemas
Sequence diagrams
 Icons & signs
Circuit schematics
 Engineering drawings
Floor plans
 Mindmaps & trees
More, with their source, at [lini.rs/gallery](https://lini.rs/gallery/). ## Colour

One file, both modes — samples/palette.lini.

Eleven named hues — `red rose orange amber lime green teal sky blue purple gray` — each in five **job-named** tiers: `wash` for backgrounds, `soft`, the bare name, `deep` for strokes, `ink` for text. The names hold across the flip — `--teal-ink` is the high-contrast tone in *both* modes, where a `light`/`dark` name would invert — which is what lets one export serve both. OKLCH underneath, so every ramp is perceptually even, and `gradient(--rose, --sky)` blends any two at a flattering angle. ## Install ```bash cargo install lini ``` ```bash lini diagram.lini -o diagram.svg # compile to SVG lini serve diagram.lini # live-reloading preview lini serve samples/ # browse and edit the bundled examples ``` Six lines — a type define, a container, and two links Lini routes for you: ``` { |svc::box| { fill: --teal-wash; stroke: --teal-ink } } |group| "Services" [ |svc#api| "API"; |svc#auth| "Auth" ] |svc#db| "Postgres" api -> db "read" auth -> db "write" ``` `{ }` is style, `[ ]` is children, and naming two nodes draws an orthogonal path between them, clear of everything in the way. The rest of the grammar is the [tour](https://lini.rs/docs/tour/language.html). ## Use it in your project - **[mdbook-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/mdbook-lini)** — ` ```lini ` fences in an mdBook, compiled to inline SVG at build time. On [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/mdbook-lini). - **[rehype-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/rehype-lini)** — the same fences anywhere [rehype](https://github.com/rehypejs/rehype) runs: Docusaurus, Next and MDX, or a bare `unified()` pipeline. A toggle reveals the source that drew each figure. On [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/rehype-lini): `npm install rehype-lini`. - **[astro-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/astro-lini)** — the Astro integration: one line in `astro.config.mjs` and every fence in the site draws. On [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/astro-lini): `npm install astro-lini`. - **[remark-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/remark-lini)** — the engine both of those run on, and the remark plugin for a pipeline that needs the figures drawn before a highlighter sees them. On [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/remark-lini-lang) as `remark-lini-lang`, since npm refuses the short name as one edit from `remark-lint`. - **[lini-wasm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/lini-wasm)** — the compiler itself, for JavaScript. One package, two builds, so it runs in Node, Bun, Deno, a bundler or a browser. This is what the integrations above ride on, and what to reach for to build one of your own. - **Editors** — search *Lini* in the extensions pane: a TextMate bundle on the [VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=monfa-red.lini) and a tree-sitter extension in [Zed's registry](https://zed.dev/extensions?query=lini). Source for both under [`editors/`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/tree/main/editors). Their word lists are generated from the compiler's own tables, so a new property highlights the day it lands. - **As a library** — `lini` is a crate as well as a binary: [docs.rs/lini](https://docs.rs/lini). ### From the community Built and maintained by their own authors, on their own release schedules. - **[obsidian-lini-view](https://github.com/FoxMaint/obsidian-lini-view)** — the Obsidian plugin: a ` ```lini ` fence draws in the note itself, live in the editor, on `lini-wasm`. ## For agents - **[`SKILL.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/SKILL.md)** — the language as a working brief: the write → compile → *look at the render* loop, every family, and the mistakes worth not making. Also served at [lini.rs/SKILL.md](https://lini.rs/SKILL.md). - **[`schema/lini.schema.json`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/schema/lini.schema.json)** — every primitive, template, role, and property with its owner, value shape, resolved default, inheritance channel, and a compiled example. Generated from the same ledger the compiler reads, and CI fails on drift. [`schema/reference.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/schema/reference.md) is the compact human mirror. - **`lini --json`** — diagnostics as JSON: stable codes, spans, and machine-applicable fixes. ## Go deeper - [The tour](https://lini.rs/docs/tour/language.html) — fourteen pages, start to finish. - [The reference](https://lini.rs/docs/reference/00-at-a-glance.html) — every property, split out of the spec. - [The gallery](https://lini.rs/gallery/) — finished figures, with the source that drew them. - [The playground](https://lini.rs/play/) — the compiler, compiled to wasm, in your browser. In this repo: [`SPEC.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/SPEC.md) is the language contract, frozen for 1.x — syntax, property names, defaults, diagnostic codes, and the theming surface stay compatible. [`ROUTING.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/ROUTING.md) is the routing contract. [`samples/`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/tree/main/samples) holds one file per feature area, and [`RELEASING.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/RELEASING.md) says how the pieces ship together. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/LICENSE).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: t.py 'snippet1' 'snippet2' ...   (\n escapes allowed via $'..' in bash)
# prints compact highlight of each snippet (original)
import sys, subprocess
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hl')
from show import compact
exe = '/workspace/executable'
args = sys.argv[1:]
if args and args[0] == '-m':
    exe = '/tmp/bin-hl/executable'
    args = args[1:]
for s in args:
    r = subprocess.run([exe, 'highlight', '-'], input=s.encode(), capture_output=True)
    out = compact(r.stdout.decode())
    print(out.replace('\n', '⏎\n   ') if '\n' in s else out, end='')
    if r.stderr or r.returncode:
        print('  STDERR:', r.stderr.decode(), 'exit', r.returncode, end='')
    print()

        print('  STDERR:', r.stderr.decode(), 'exit', r.returncode, end='')

input.content: #!/usr/bin/env python3 # brute-force words of length n over alphabet in a context; print words whose classification is not the default import sys, itertools, string, re, subprocess sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hl') from show import compact n = int(sys.argv[1]) ctx = sys.argv[2] alpha = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else string.ascii_lowercase fmts = {'bar': '|%s|', 'prop': '%s: 1', 'val': 'x: %s', 'call': 'x: %s(1)', 'norm': '%s'} default = {'bar': 'type-user', 'prop': 'prop-user', 'val': None, 'call': None, 'norm': None} fmt = fmts[ctx] CH = 20000 it = (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n)) found = [] while True: chunk = list(itertools.islice(it, CH)) if not chunk: break src = '\n'.join(fmt % w for w in chunk) + '\n' r = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable', 'highlight', '-'], input=src.encode(), capture_output=True) lines = r.stdout.decode().split('\n') for w, line in zip(chunk, lines): m = re.findall(r'' + re.escape(w) + '', line) k = m[0] if m else None if k != default[ctx]: found.append((w, k)) for w, k in found: print(w, k)

            if bad < 10:

content.text:
I've implemented `lini highlight` in `src/highlight.rs`, and its output matches the original byte-for-byte on everything I tested. It's committed on branch `worktree-agent-a784900525c4e6863` (bba3247); no other file was changed.

**Results (all compared with `cmpw.py`):**
- **Asset corpus:** 246/246 (`test_doc_examples`, `blocks`, `test_samples`).
- **Snippet corpus:** 484/484. That's 384 targeted snippets plus 100 randomly mutated multi-line documents, in `/tmp/hl/corpus/`.
- **CRLF and tab-indented copies of every asset:** 492/492, in `/tmp/hl/crlf/`.
- **Exhaustive runs:** every combination of small character and token sets up to length 5–6, about 1.2M lines, found 0 differences.
- **Random fuzzing:** about 250k random and mutated lines found 0 differences, including NBSP/NEL/U+2028, astral characters, NUL, form feed and vertical tab.

**How the original behaves.** It never fails and keeps every byte, escaping `& < > "` (but not `'`). It has three modes, and a newline resets all of them:
- **Structural (default):**
  - A name followed by optional spaces/tabs and a single `:` is `prop` or `prop-user`, unless a side word follows directly (`a:left` stays plain).
  - Link operators are an optional head (`<>` `<` `>` `*`), then `-`, `--`, `---` or `~`, then an optional tail; `&` is also an operator.
  - Also recognised: `--var`, `#hex` (exactly 3/4/6/8 digits), unsigned numbers (`+5` is a number, `-5` is an operator then a number).
  - `.class`, and bare `left`/`right`/`top`/`bottom` as `const`, only count when the previous character isn't `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`.
  - `:` switches to value mode and `|` starts a bar run.
- **Value (after `:`, until `;`, `}`, `]` or end of line):**
  - Numbers may be signed, and `( ) ,` are punct.
  - A builder name like `rgb` is `type` when `(` follows, even across spaces, tabs, newlines or form feed (not NBSP or vertical tab).
  - The keyword list is checked before the colour list.
  - Everything else is plain, including `{`, `|`, `:`, classes and link operators.
- **Bars (`|…|` on one line):** names are `type` or `type-user`, a name right after `#` is always `type`, `::` is an operator, and `.class` counts. Strings, comments and numbers aren't recognised inside bars.
- **Strings and comments:** both stop at the newline. A backslash escapes the next character except a newline, and a trailing backslash stays inside the string.

**Word lists.** Running `executable serve DIR` serves a playground page that contains the original's own JavaScript copy of the highlighter, including its generated word lists. That is the program's own output, not decompilation, but you may want to confirm you're comfortable with that reading of the rules. I took the lists from it (112 types, 113 properties, 62 keywords, 25 colours, 10 builder functions) and checked every word against the binary. The 113 properties are exactly the set of `prop_*.lini` files. The JavaScript differs from the binary in two places, and I followed the binary in both:
- A string ending in a backslash keeps the backslash inside the span.
- The builder `(` lookahead skips newlines but not NBSP.

**Remaining mismatches, all outside `highlight.rs` and left alone as instructed:**
1. **Invalid UTF-8 input (`read_input` in `main.rs`, affects every subcommand):**
   - For a file, the original prints `error: <path>: stream did not contain valid UTF-8` and exits 2. Ours decodes it lossily and carries on.
   - For stdin, the original prints `error: failed to read stdin: stream did not contain valid UTF-8`. Ours prints `error: <stdin>: …`.
2. **Argument handling in `cli.rs`:**
   - `highlight -- FILE` is accepted by the original and rejected by ours.
   - `--css=1` and `--css --css` give different error messages from the original's.

The test scripts are in `/tmp/hl/`: `check_all.sh` for the snippets plus assets, `fuzz3.py` and `mfuzz.py` for fuzzing, and `exh.py` / `exht.py` for the exhaustive runs.
